answer_text:
Assume \(\varphi\) is sufficiently regular so that the integral manipulations below are valid. First note that at \(x=0\),

\[
0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\varphi(0)\,d\theta=\varphi(0),
\]

so \(\varphi(0)=0\).

Now take \(x>0\). In the integral, set

\[
t=x\sin\theta.
\]

Then \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(x\), and

\[
dt=x\cos\theta\,d\theta=x\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta
=x\sqrt{1-\frac{t^2}{x^2}}\,d\theta
=\sqrt{x^2-t^2}\,d\theta.
\]

Hence

\[
d\theta=\frac{dt}{\sqrt{x^2-t^2}},
\]

and the equation becomes

\[
x^2=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^x \frac{\varphi(t)}{\sqrt{x^2-t^2}}\,dt.
\]

Now set

\[
y=x^2,\qquad u=t^2.
\]

Then \(t=\sqrt{u}\), \(dt=\frac{du}{2\sqrt{u}}\), and

\[
\sqrt{x^2-t^2}=\sqrt{y-u}.
\]

Define

\[
F(u)=\frac{\varphi(\sqrt{u})}{\sqrt{u}}.
\]

Then

\[
y=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^y \frac{F(u)}{\sqrt{y-u}}\,du,
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\int_0^y \frac{F(u)}{\sqrt{y-u}}\,du=\pi y.
\]

This is an Abel integral equation. To invert it, define

\[
G(y)=\int_0^y \frac{F(u)}{\sqrt{y-u}}\,du=\pi y.
\]

Now consider

\[
H(y)=\int_0^y \frac{G(s)}{\sqrt{y-s}}\,ds.
\]

Using \(G(s)=\pi s\),

\[
H(y)=\int_0^y \frac{\pi s}{\sqrt{y-s}}\,ds.
\]

On the other hand, substituting the definition of \(G\),

\[
H(y)=\int_0^y \int_0^s
\frac{F(u)}{\sqrt{s-u}}\,du\,\frac{ds}{\sqrt{y-s}}.
\]

Interchanging the order of integration,

\[
H(y)=\int_0^y F(u)
\left(\int_u^y \frac{ds}{\sqrt{(s-u)(y-s)}}\right)du.
\]

The inner integral is standard:

\[
\int_u^y \frac{ds}{\sqrt{(s-u)(y-s)}}=\pi.
\]

Therefore,

\[
H(y)=\pi\int_0^y F(u)\,du.
\]

But we also computed

\[
H(y)=\int_0^y \frac{\pi s}{\sqrt{y-s}}\,ds
=\frac{4\pi}{3}y^{3/2}.
\]

Differentiating both expressions for \(H(y)\),

\[
\pi F(y)=\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}y^{3/2}\right)
=2\pi\sqrt{y}.
\]

Thus

\[
F(y)=2\sqrt{y}.
\]

Recall that

\[
F(y)=\frac{\varphi(\sqrt{y})}{\sqrt{y}}.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{\varphi(\sqrt{y})}{\sqrt{y}}=2\sqrt{y},
\]

so

\[
\varphi(\sqrt{y})=2y.
\]

Letting \(x=\sqrt{y}\), we obtain

\[
\varphi(x)=2x^2.
\]

Finally, check:

\[
\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\varphi(x\sin\theta)\,d\theta
=
\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}2x^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac{4x^2}{\pi}\cdot \frac{\pi}{4}
=
x^2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\varphi(x)=2x^2}
\]

for \(x\ge 0\). If the equation is intended for all real \(x\), the same formula gives \(\varphi(x)=2x^2\) for all real \(x\).
